paras: The threatened lynching of Dave and Albert Lewis took place in Kentucky in August 1888, when a mob threatened to lynch two young men charged with killing their cousin. The two were taken to the jail at Mt. Sterling because Morgan county had no place secure enough to protect them, and no attack on them was reported. Kentucky papers said the pair had murdered both a young woman and their cousin, while the wire story behind the case gave a different account of who was charged with what.

According to a Mount Sterling dispatch of August 11, Joe Lewis had been charged with the murder of a Miss Auxier in Morgan county that spring and had evaded the officers. He returned to his home three weeks before the dispatch, announced that he would turn State's evidence, and then disappeared. His body was found on August 10 with two bullet holes in the back of the head; he had been dragged about a hundred yards and thrown over a precipice, given as 75 feet high in some versions and 25 in another.

Dave and Al Lewis were charged with the killing, and one version said they had been arrested. The dispatch described them as two cousins of the dead man, with a brother also charged, aged 16, 18 and 20, though another printing called them 'his cousin and brother,' aged 19 and 21.

A week later the Maysville Evening Bulletin reported that 'Morehead, Ky., people' had caught Dave and Albert Lewis and were threatening a lynching. The Semi-Weekly Interior Journal of Stanford added that the two, aged 14 and 19, had been brought to Mt. Sterling and lodged in jail, since there was no secure place in Morgan county to protect them from 'the mob, who have threatened to lynch them.' Neither paper gave the size of the mob or named any of its members.
No report of an attack on the jail, an inquest into Joe Lewis's death, or a trial of the accused was found in the coverage.

Only two Kentucky papers reported the threat, and both described the accused in the same words, as men 'who murdered a young lady and their cousin, Henry Lewis.' The Maysville Evening Bulletin placed the item in its 'Pointed Paragraphs' column and treated the mob with irony, writing that 'On the theory that "like cures like"' the Morehead people meant to mend 'the fracture in their laws' with 'another lynching bee.' The Stanford paper ran a flat one-sentence item among its news briefs, stating the murders as fact.

Outside Kentucky, the story appeared only as the Mount Sterling wire on Joe Lewis's death, headed 'A Murderer Killed' in the Alexandria Gazette and 'A Foul Deed' in the Wichita Eagle. The Washington Critic and the Brookhaven Leader in Mississippi carried shorter versions among their news briefs, and none of these wire printings mentioned a mob. No paper gave the race of any of the Lewises.

The Kentucky papers named the murdered cousin Henry Lewis and said Dave and Albert had also killed the young woman, while the earlier and more detailed wire reports named him Joe Lewis and said he himself had been charged with Miss Auxier's murder. The two Kentucky items share their wording and may compress the wire story, and the wire's versions agree with one another on the name. The papers also differ on the ages of the accused, on whether a brother was charged with them, and on whether they were caught at Morehead or in Morgan county.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Dave and Albert Lewis
bases: Two Kentucky papers report that a mob threatened to lynch Dave and Albert Lewis, who were then jailed at Mt. Sterling for their protection; no attack on them is reported (A5, A6).

The papers report only a threat by a mob of unstated size, made on the ground that the two were murderers, and the accused were moved to a jail out of reach; no one is reported killed by the mob (A5, A6). The killing of Joe Lewis that the two were charged with is reported as the work of his kin, not of a mob acting as justice (A1, A2, A3).

The threat appears only in two Kentucky papers whose identical wording ('who murdered a young lady and their cousin, Henry Lewis') points to one common item, though A6 adds details (A5, A6); the wire reports confirm the arrest and charge but say nothing of a mob (A1, A2, A3).

accounts.label: Mount Sterling wire
accounts.gist: Joe Lewis, charged with Miss Auxier's murder, returned home, said he would turn State's evidence and vanished; his body was found shot and thrown over a precipice, and Dave and Al Lewis were charged.

accounts.label: Kentucky papers
accounts.gist: Dave and Albert Lewis, who 'murdered a young lady and their cousin, Henry Lewis,' were caught and threatened with lynching, and were taken to the Mt. Sterling jail for safety.

framing.detail: The Maysville Evening Bulletin wrote with irony that the Morehead people, 'On the theory that "like cures like,"' meant to mend their broken laws with 'another lynching bee.'
The Semi-Weekly Interior Journal ran a plain one-sentence item stating the murders as fact and noting the move to the Mt. Sterling jail.
Out-of-state papers ran the Mount Sterling wire under headlines such as 'A Murderer Killed' and 'A Foul Deed,' with no mention of a mob.

conflicts.note: The wire versions are earlier and more detailed and agree with one another; the two Kentucky items share one wording.

info: The threat was reported between August 18 and August 21, 1888; the killing the two were charged with was discovered on August 10, 1888.
Morehead, Ky., where 'people' caught the two (A5); the crime was placed in Morgan county and the two were jailed at Mt. Sterling (A6).
Dave and Albert (Al) Lewis, the targets of the threat; ages given variously as 14 and 19 (A6), 16 and 18 with a 20-year-old brother (A1, A3), or 19 and 21 (A2). No race is given.

Kentucky papers say they 'murdered a young lady and their cousin, Henry Lewis' (A5, A6); the wire says they were charged with killing Joe Lewis, himself charged with murdering Miss Auxier, after he said he would turn State's evidence (A1, A2).
'Morehead, Ky., people' (A5); 'the mob' (A6). No one is named.
Held in the Mt. Sterling jail; no lynching reported.
